subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 17-year-old high-school basketball player collapses and loses consciousness while sprinting up the court during a game. He had complained of dizziness moments earlier, and resuscitation is unsuccessful. Autopsy reveals marked thickening of the interventricular septum with myofibrillar disarray and interstitial fibrosis on histology. His father was diagnosed with the same inherited cardiac condition.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

options.text: Dilated cardiomyopathy due to a titin (TTN) mutation

explanation_correct: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is 60–70% familial in an autosomal dominant pattern, most commonly due to mutations in genes encoding sarcomeric proteins such as myosin binding protein C and β-myosin heavy chain. It causes syncope during exercise and may lead to sudden death in young athletes from ventricular arrhythmia. Grossly the ventricle is thickened (often with septal predominance), and histology shows myofibrillar disarray and fibrosis.

explanation_incorrect.A: Titin mutations cause familial dilated cardiomyopathy, which shows a dilated, ballooning-appearing heart with eccentric hypertrophy and systolic dysfunction, not septal thickening with disarray.
explanation_incorrect.B: Amyloidosis causes a restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy with a low-voltage ECG despite a thick myocardium, typically in older adults, and does not show myofibrillar disarray.
explanation_incorrect.C: Endocardial fibroelastosis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy with thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium of young children, not an autosomal dominant sarcomeric disorder of adolescents.
explanation_incorrect.E: Stress cardiomyopathy causes ventricular apical ballooning after increased sympathetic stimulation (eg, emotional stress) and is not inherited; it does not cause septal hypertrophy with disarray.

educationalObjective: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is the classic cause of exercise-related syncope and sudden death in young athletes and is inherited autosomal dominantly via sarcomeric protein mutations.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 58-year-old man with known hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy is started on furosemide and isosorbide dinitrate by his primary care physician for mild ankle swelling. He returns 2 weeks later with worsening exertional dyspnea and a near-syncopal episode while climbing stairs. Examination now shows a louder systolic murmur at the left sternal border, and the murmur intensifies when he stands up.
question: Which of the following best explains this patient's deterioration after starting the new medications?

options.text: Reduced preload narrowed the left ventricular cavity and worsened outflow tract obstruction
Reduced myocardial contractility caused ventricular dilation and worsening mitral regurgitation
The medications triggered coronary artery vasospasm
The medications uncovered significant epicardial coronary artery stenosis

explanation_correct: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, drugs that decrease preload (eg, diuretics, vasodilators) must be avoided: reducing LV filling volume makes the hypertrophied septum and systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve obstruct the outflow tract more severely, worsening dyspnea and syncope. Appropriate treatment is β-blockers or nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers (eg, verapamil), and ICD placement if high risk.

explanation_incorrect.B: Decreasing contractility is actually the therapeutic goal in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy (achieved with β-blockers or verapamil) because it lessens outflow obstruction; it is not the effect of furosemide or nitrates.
explanation_incorrect.C: Coronary vasospasm causes variant angina with transient ST elevation, not a louder left sternal border systolic murmur and positional outflow obstruction physiology.
explanation_incorrect.D: Exertional near-syncope in this patient is explained by dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction, not by new epicardial coronary stenosis; the murmur behavior on standing points to a preload-dependent obstructive lesion.
explanation_incorrect.E: Loop diuretic hypokalemia can cause ventricular arrhythmias, but it would not produce a louder outflow murmur that intensifies on standing, which is the hallmark of worsening obstruction.

educationalObjective: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, avoid preload-reducing drugs (diuretics, vasodilators); treat with β-blockers or nondihydropyridine Ca2+ channel blockers.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 24-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnea and a syncopal episode that occurred while playing recreational basketball. Echocardiography shows asymmetric septal hypertrophy and abnormal anterior movement of the mitral valve leaflet toward the hypertrophied interventricular septum during systole, accompanied by a jet of mitral regurgitation.
question: Which of the following sequences best explains this patient's dyspnea and syncope?

options.text: Mitral leaflet coaptation is impaired, causing mitral stenosis, reduced LA emptying, and pulmonary edema
Septal hypertrophy obstructs the right ventricular outflow tract, reducing pulmonary blood flow and causing hypoxemia
Diastolic collapse of the ventricle reduces filling and causes a fall in cardiac output during exercise
Impaired ventricular relaxation raises end-diastolic pressure, causing orthopnea and paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea
Systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve contributes to LV outflow tract obstruction, reducing forward flow and causing dyspnea and syncope

explanation_correct: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy is classified as hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy when the LV outflow tract is obstructed. Asymmetric septal hypertrophy plus systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve leads to outflow obstruction, which leads to dyspnea and possible syncope, particularly during exertion when obstruction worsens. The same impaired mitral valve closure produces the accompanying mitral regurgitation jet.

explanation_incorrect.A: Impaired mitral valve closure in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes mitral regurgitation, not mitral stenosis; the syncope mechanism is outflow tract obstruction rather than restricted LA emptying.
explanation_incorrect.B: In hypertrophic cardiomyopathy the obstruction is in the left ventricular outflow tract; the right ventricular outflow tract and pulmonary blood flow are not the primary sites of obstruction.
explanation_incorrect.C: Diastolic collapse of a ventricular chamber is a finding of cardiac tamponade on echocardiography, not the mechanism of exertional syncope in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
explanation_incorrect.D: Diastolic dysfunction with elevated end-diastolic pressure does occur in hypertrophic cardiomyopathy and contributes to dyspnea, but the exertional syncope is best explained by dynamic LV outflow tract obstruction.

educationalObjective: Asymmetric septal hypertrophy with systolic anterior motion of the mitral valve causes LV outflow obstruction, leading to dyspnea and possible syncope in hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 70-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and bilateral leg swelling. Echocardiography shows a thick-walled left ventricle with preserved ejection fraction and diastolic dysfunction. Electrocardiogram unexpectedly shows low-voltage QRS complexes despite the increased myocardial thickness on echocardiography. Endomyocardial biopsy shows amorphous eosinophilic deposits within the myocardium.
question: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?
explanation_correct: Cardiac amyloidosis is a restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy causing diastolic dysfunction, and it classically produces a low-voltage ECG despite a thick myocardium — a particularly characteristic feature of amyloidosis. The amorphous eosinophilic deposits on biopsy are consistent with amyloid protein deposition.

explanation_incorrect.A: Löffler endocarditis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy associated with hypereosinophilic syndrome, with eosinophilic infiltrates in the myocardium; it is not the classic cause of low-voltage ECG despite a thick myocardium.
explanation_incorrect.C: Postradiation fibrosis is a cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy but requires a history of mediastinal or chest radiation and does not characteristically produce the striking low-voltage ECG with thick walls.
explanation_incorrect.D: Endocardial fibroelastosis features thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium of young children, not an elderly adult with biopsy-proven amorphous deposits and a low-voltage ECG.
explanation_incorrect.E: Hypertrophic cardiomyopathy causes a thick myocardium with concentric hypertrophy and diastolic dysfunction, but it is a sarcomeric disease with myofibrillar disarray, not amorphous deposits, and does not characteristically show low-voltage QRS complexes.

educationalObjective: A low-voltage ECG despite a thick myocardium, especially with restrictive physiology, points particularly to amyloidosis.

subject: Cardiovascular
vignette: A 45-year-old man presents with progressive exertional dyspnea and fatigue. Echocardiography shows a stiff ventricle with impaired filling and preserved ejection fraction. Laboratory evaluation reveals a white blood cell count of 28,000/mm³ with 45% eosinophils, and he is diagnosed with hypereosinophilic syndrome. Endomyocardial biopsy is performed.
question: Which of the following findings is most likely on myocardial biopsy?

options.text: Amorphous eosinophilic deposits with apple-green birefringence under polarized light
Thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium

explanation_correct: Löffler endocarditis is a restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy associated with hypereosinophilic syndrome; histology shows eosinophilic infiltrates in the myocardium. Restrictive cardiomyopathies share diastolic dysfunction as the common physiologic consequence.

explanation_incorrect.A: Amorphous deposits with apple-green birefringence on polarized light microscopy indicate amyloid, a separate cause of restrictive cardiomyopathy not driven by hypereosinophilia.
explanation_incorrect.B: Noncaseating granulomas characterize cardiac sarcoidosis, another cause of restrictive/infiltrative cardiomyopathy, but they are not eosinophilic infiltrates and are not tied to hypereosinophilic syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.D: Thick fibroelastic tissue in the endocardium describes endocardial fibroelastosis, which occurs in young children rather than an adult with hypereosinophilic syndrome.
explanation_incorrect.E: Myofibrillar disarray with fibrosis is the histology of hypertrophic cardiomyopathy, a diastolic dysfunction disease but not an infiltrative/eosinophilic process.

educationalObjective: Löffler endocarditis is a restrictive cardiomyopathy associated with hypereosinophilic syndrome and eosinophilic infiltrates in the myocardium.
